title: Brahma medhavā: the third trisuparṇa
theme: The third trisuparṇa: brahman is reached by sacrifice; two Ṛgvedic verses praising Soma and the swan who dwells everywhere; the streams of ghee and the golden reed on which the fine-winged bird sits; and the brāhmaṇa lines.

words.gram: as printed (for the instr./nom. of medhavat)
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «मेधवा मेधो यज्ञः सोऽस्यास्तीति मेधवत्» — medha is sacrifice; medhavat, having sacrifice
Bhāskara: «मेधो यज्ञो ज्योतिष्टोमादिस् तद्वत् तदनुष्ठानेन प्राप्यते ज्ञायते वा न विना कर्मणा» — reached or known by performing sacrifices such as the jyotiṣṭoma, not without action
Bhāskara: «सोमयागः सर्वं प्रवित्रमतिशेत इति» — the soma sacrifice surpasses every purifier

words.meaning: born of the cows (or of the earth)

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «ऋग्वेदरूपाय त्वा व्यत्ययेन तुभ्यमियं समिदग्नौ निक्षिप्यत इति शेषः» — to you who are the Ṛgveda this fuel-stick is laid in the fire

words.gram: pron. 2nd pers. acc. sg. (for the dative)

words.role: main verb; subject the streams of ghee

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «धीयन्ते पीयन्ते देवैरिति धेनाः» — dhenāḥ, because the gods drink them
The anonymous commentator: «अन्तर्हृदा त्द्दत्कोशवर्तिना» — dwelling in the sheath of the heart
The anonymous commentator: offered with inward attention they are pure, otherwise not
The anonymous commentator: I will give them to all the gods
The anonymous commentator: «हिरण्ययो ज्योतिर्मयः» — made of light
The anonymous commentator: read, with a change of letter, as one rich in substance («वेतसो वर्णव्यत्ययेन वेदस्वान्बहुद्रव्यवान्»)
The anonymous commentator: who makes sweet happiness such as heaven
The anonymous commentator: «सर्वप्राणिदेहनीडाश्रयत्वेन कुलायी» — nesting, because the bodies of all beings are his nests
The anonymous commentator: «हरन्ति पापानि स्मरणमात्रेणेति हरयः» — the seven ṛṣis, who take away sins by being remembered
Sāyaṇa: «वेदशास्त्रतदनुष्ठानपरो ब्राह्मणोऽभिषिक्तो राजा वा वीरः» — a brāhmaṇa devoted to the Veda and its practice, or an anointed king; Bhāskara: «गुणवान् पुत्रो वीरः» — a virtuous son
constantly repeat it (Sāyaṇa on the first trisuparṇa)
the soma sacrifice (Sāyaṇa), or the supreme god Soma (Bhāskara), as on the first trisuparṇa
a row of diners at a śrāddha (Bhāskara, on the first trisuparṇa)

sandhi.type: final m before a vowel; i-visarga before a voiced sound
sandhi.rule: m joined to the vowel; ṛṣiḥ + viprāṇām → ṛṣir viprāṇām.
The m becomes anusvāra before s (P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः)); the Taittirīya recitation writes it ग्.

sandhi.type: final m before a vowel; i + e
sandhi.rule: ati + eti → atyeti (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)), a preverb joined to its verb.
t becomes d before a voiced sound, and the h that follows may become dh (P. 8.4.62 (झयो होऽन्यतरस्याम्)).
antaḥ stands for antar, whose r shows before h.
maddhye + āsām → maddhya āsām: e becomes ay and the y drops (P. 6.1.78 (एचोऽयवायावः), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
A t may be inserted between final n and s (P. 8.3.30 (नश्च)).

sandhi.type: n after a short vowel before a vowel
sandhi.rule: The n is doubled (P. 8.3.32 (ङमो ह्रस्वादचि ङमुण्नित्यम्)).
brāhmaṇāḥ + trisuparṇam → brāhmaṇās trisuparṇam: the visarga becomes s before t (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)).
ā and sahasrāt are written as one; final t stays before p.

morphology.note: From medhavat ‘having sacrifice’ (Sāyaṇa); Bhāskara explains the ending ā as the case ending of the vat-stem replaced by the rule P. 7.1.39 (सुपां सुलुक्पूर्वसवर्णाऽऽच्छेयाडाड्यायाजालः).
The Ānandāśrama print marks this reading as adopted from two manuscripts, where others read ṛce again (see flags).
The preverb ati written with its verb; Soma ‘goes through’ the filter.

translation.literal: Brahman by sacrifice; sweetness by sacrifice; brahman itself, sweetness, by sacrifice. The brahman among the gods, the path-finder among poets, the seer among the inspired, the buffalo among wild beasts, the falcon among birds of prey, the axe among woods — Soma goes through the filter, singing. The swan dwelling in the bright, the Vasu dwelling in the mid-air, the offerer seated at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house, dwelling among men, in the choicest place, in the right order, in the sky; born of the waters, of the cows, of the right order, of the rock — the right order, great. For the verse, you; for brightness, you; the fuel-stick. They flow like rivers, streams, purified within, by heart and mind; I behold the streams of ghee. A golden reed in the middle of them; on it the fine-winged one, honey-maker, nesting, sits apportioning honey to the deities; on its bank sit the seven bay ones, milking the svadhā, the stream of the deathless. Whoever gives this trisuparṇa unasked to a brāhmaṇa — these truly destroy [the sin of] killing a hero. The brāhmaṇas who recite the trisuparṇa attain soma. They purify the row up to a thousand. Om.
translation.readable: Brahman is reached through sacrifice; so is the sweet; so is Brahman itself, the sweet. As the chief priest among the gods, the path-finder among poets, the buffalo among beasts, the falcon among birds, the axe among the trees, so Soma passes singing through the filter. The swan in the bright sky, the god in mid-air, the priest at the altar, the guest in the house, at home among men and in the highest place, in the true order and in the sky, born of water, earth, truth and rock — he is the great order. For the verse and for its brightness, this fuel-stick. The streams of ghee, made pure within by the heart and the mind, flow like rivers, and I watch them. In their midst stands a golden reed; on it sits the fine-winged bird that makes honey and shares it with the gods; on its bank sit the seven, drawing out the stream of the deathless. The text then promises, as before, that those who teach this unasked destroy the sin of killing a hero, attain soma, and purify a row of a thousand. Om.

anvaya: ब्रह्म मेधवा [लभ्यते] । मधु मेधवा । ब्रह्मम् एव मधु मेधवा । देवानाम् ब्रह्मा, कवीनाम् पदवीः, विप्राणाम् ऋषिः, मृगाणाम् महिषः, गृद्ध्राणाम् श्येनः, वनानाम् स्वधितिः [इव] सोमः रेभन् पवित्रम् अत्येति । हंसः शुचिषत् … ऋतम् बृहत् । ऋचे त्वा, रुचे त्वा, समित् [अग्नौ निक्षिप्यते] । अन्तः हृदा मनसा पूयमानाः धेनाः सरितः न स्रवन्ति । घृतस्य धाराः अभिचाकशीमि । आसाम् मद्ध्ये हिरण्ययः वेतसः [अस्ति] । तस्मिन् मधुकृत् कुलायी सुपर्णः देवताभ्यः मधु भजन् आस्ते । तस्य तीरे सप्त हरयः अमृतस्य धाराम् स्वधाम् दुहानाः आसते । यः इदम् त्रिसुपर्णम् … । ओम् ।
syntax: Three verbless statements with medhavā; a verse listing the best of each kind (ṣaṣṭhī of the group with a nominative) and ending in a finite verb (atyeti); a verse of nominative epithets ending in ṛtaṃ bṛhat; two datives with tvā and a nominative samit, the verb supplied; a sequence of clauses with stream-imagery: a plural verb (sravanti), a first-person verb (abhicākaśīmi), a verbless statement (hiraṇyayo vetasaḥ …), and two sentences with āste / āsate. Then the brāhmaṇa.

ambiguities.note: Sāyaṇa and the anonymous commentator: medha is sacrifice, so brahman is reached by those who perform sacrifice; Bhāskara: by action such as the jyotiṣṭoma, and not without it («न विना कर्मणा»). He sets the three trisuparṇa in order: meditation, knowledge, action (see commentary).

ambiguities.topic: the golden reed and the bird
ambiguities.note: The anonymous commentator reads the reed as the fire in which the streams are offered and the fine-winged one as the trisuparṇa, the supreme self, apportioning the offerings to the gods, with the seven ṛṣis around him; the text leaves the image without a gloss of its own.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Prose formulas; two Ṛgvedic verses (Bhāskara: «ब्रह्मा देवानामिति त्रिष्टुप्», «हंसश्शुचिषदित्य् अतिजगती»); verse lines of the streams and the reed; and the brāhmaṇa in prose.

beginner: The third trisuparṇa says that Brahman, the sweet, is reached through sacrifice. One commentator, Bhāskara, sees an order in the three: the first spoke of meditation, the second of knowledge, the third of action. Two old verses follow. The first lists the best of every kind — the chief priest among the gods, the falcon among birds, the axe among the trees — and says Soma passes singing through the filter. The second calls the divine swan the one who lives everywhere: in the bright sky, at the altar, in the house, among people. Then comes a picture: streams of ghee, made pure by the heart and mind, flowing like rivers, a golden reed in their midst, and on it a bird that makes honey and shares it with the gods. The text ends with its usual promise to those who teach and recite it.
analogy: Like three ways to the same house — studying the map, knowing the road, and walking it — each called by the same name.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That brahman, the sweet, is reached by sacrifice; it praises Soma among the best of all kinds and the swan who dwells everywhere; it offers the fuel-stick to the verse and to brightness; it describes the streams of ghee, the golden reed in their midst and the fine-winged bird on it, with the seven on its bank; and it states the reward of the trisuparṇa.

commentary.q: How do the three trisuparṇa differ?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara: the first taught meditation as the means of reaching the highest, the second knowledge, and the third now teaches action: «तत्र प्रथमे उपासना परप्राप्तिहेतुरुक्ता । द्वितीये ज्ञानम् । इदानीं कर्मणः परप्राप्तिसाधनत्वमुच्यते». Sāyaṇa: medha is sacrifice, and the knowledge of brahman comes after the desire to know, which sacrifice and giving produce («यज्ञदानादिनाध्यविविदिषा»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the supreme self, from whom the three ‘fine-winged ones’ arise — Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara, or other triads — and the text is called by its name because it states his greatness: «तन्महिमप्रतिपादकत्वादयं ग्रन्थोऽपि त्रिसुपर्णशब्देनोपचर्यते».

commentary.q: Who are the seven on the bank?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the seven ṛṣis around the Lord, called hari because remembering them takes away sin: «हरन्ति पापानि स्मरणमात्रेणेति हरयः».

commentary.q: Who is the ‘hero’ whose killing is named?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa: a brāhmaṇa devoted to the Veda and its practice, or an anointed king (vīra); Bhāskara: a virtuous son, or, as others say, an anointed kṣatriya («गुणवान् पुत्रो वीरः । अभिषिक्तः क्षत्रिय इत्यन्ये»). The anonymous commentator ranks the three sins of the three trisuparṇa in ascending gravity (10.41).

commentary.q: Where are the two Ṛgvedic verses explained?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa says the verses brahmā devānām and haṃsaḥ śuciṣat were explained in the anuvāka aṇor aṇīyān: «इत्यादिके द्वे ऋचावणोरणीयानित्यनुवाके व्याख्याते». The anonymous commentator says the same of them: «ब्रह्मा देवानां ह ँसः शुचिषदिति द्वे ऋचावणोरणीयानित्यस्मिन्ननुवाके व्याख्याते».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources. Bhāskara’s ordering of meditation, knowledge and action, and his insistence that brahman is not reached without action, is his own reading; the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read medhavā of sacrifice that leads to the desire to know. Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

parallels.note: The Kaṭha Upaniṣad has the same verse (also Ṛgveda 4.40.5), of the self that dwells in all.

contemporary.text: Bhāskara reads the three passages as three means to one end — attention, understanding and action. Whether one approaches a goal by contemplating it, by learning about it or by working for it, each can be honoured. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: The verse names the best of each kind. What would you name as ‘the best’ of a few things you know well?
reflect.deeper: Bhāskara says brahman is not reached without action. How does doing something change what one understands about it?
reflect.practice: Pick one thing you understand well and do one small act that puts it into practice today.

references.text: Sāyaṇa (his 50) and Bhāskara (his 50) comment on this anuvāka; the concordance maps both correctly. The verse brahmā devānām is also Ṛgveda 9.96.6, and the lines from ghṛtasya dhārā to the golden reed recall Ṛgveda 4.58.5; the edition’s parallel sources do not contain those maṇḍalas.
The effects claimed for giving and reciting the trisuparṇa are the text’s own and are reported as such.

flags.note: ṛce tvā ruce tvā: the Tirupati e-text reads ṛce tvā ṛce tvā; the Ānandāśrama print marks ruce as adopted from two manuscripts while others read ṛce (corrections.json, review). The base reading ruce is kept.

maddhye / madhye and gṛddhrāṇām / gṛdhrāṇām: the two other witnesses agree on the single consonant where the base doubles it (corrections.json, review); a spelling of the recitation, the words unchanged.
The image of the streams, the reed and the bird is read by the anonymous commentator as the fire-offering and the supreme self; other readings are possible.
